en: A security lock that stops the steering wheel turning when the key is removed.
UK roads marked with red lines where stopping and parking are tightly restricted.
The official owner’s manual from the car maker explaining controls and systems.
The official UK rules and advice for road users.
Zigzag road markings near crossings; parking and waiting there is restricted.
Tyres with too little air; can raise fuel use and affect braking.
The padded support behind your head on the seat, often called a headrest.
A driver-assistance feature that detects tired driving and alerts you.
ABS: brakes that help stop the wheels locking under hard braking.
A steering column designed to fold in a crash to reduce injury.
A council tip or recycling centre that accepts items like used engine oil.
Permanently marking the vehicle’s number plate onto glass or parts.
UK annual roadworthiness tests (MOT) checking safety and emissions.
A special seat that holds a child safely with the correct restraints.
Air and noise pollution in towns and cities, often from traffic.
Run the engine at very high revs, which wastes fuel and can cause wear.
How the tyre rubber wears down; uneven wear can signal a fault.
Look far ahead and prepare early for what other vehicles will do.
Cruise control that also adjusts speed to keep a gap from the vehicle ahead.
A child seat that faces backwards, safer for infants in a crash.
A safety cushion that inflates quickly in a crash to protect occupants.
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation: chest compressions (and breaths) to help someone not breathing.
Not awake and not responding; may need emergency help.
Automated external defibrillator: a device that can shock the heart back to rhythm.
People trained to give basic emergency care before professionals arrive.
Emergency medical staff who treat patients at the scene and in ambulances.
Hazardous materials (chemicals, fuels, etc.) needing special transport rules.
Warning symbols or plates that show a load’s danger type.
Electronic signs that change to show live warnings or instructions.
Eight-sided shape; in the UK the STOP sign is octagonal.
A warning that two bends follow closely, one after the other.
A warning that the road surface may be slippery.
A warning that the carriageway becomes narrower ahead.
The period of fading light after sunset when visibility drops.
Strong wind blowing across the road from the side, which can push a vehicle off its line.
High-visibility clothing (bright/reflective) that makes a person easier to see, especially in poor light.
How much air is in each tyre; incorrect pressure affects handling, braking, and tyre wear.
The clear space you keep ahead of your vehicle so you can stop safely if traffic slows or stops.
A system that sends power to all four wheels to improve grip, especially on slippery or uneven surfaces.
To start moving from a stopped position, such as pulling away from the kerb or after waiting.
The top layer of the road that tyres touch (e.g. tarmac, snow, ice, or loose gravel).
A triangular road sign that warns of a danger or difficult situation ahead on the road.
Electronic Stability Control: a system that helps keep the car stable if wheels start to lose grip.
How well the tyres hold onto the road surface without sliding.
The springs and related parts that connect the wheels to the car body and absorb bumps.
The pipes and parts that carry waste gases from the engine out of the vehicle.
A person riding a motorcycle; they can be less stable and harder to see than cars.
Water covering part of the road after heavy rain or flooding, which can wet the brakes.
Headlights on their brightest, longest setting; can dazzle others, so not for use in fog or when meeting traffic.
The storage compartment at the back of a car (called the trunk in some countries).
The radio antenna on a vehicle, often a thin rod on the roof or rear.
The protective bar at the front or rear of a vehicle designed to absorb minor impacts.
A lower gear ratio that gives more engine control at slower speeds, often used on hills.
A higher gear used for faster cruising, with less engine braking effect than a low gear.
A slow agricultural vehicle often seen on country roads; overtaking needs clear space and time.
Headlights on their brightest, longest setting; must be dipped so you do not dazzle other drivers.
Switch from full beam to dipped (lower) beam so oncoming or overtaking drivers are not dazzled.
A slow vehicle that cleans the road surface; give it space when passing.
People riding motorcycles; they can be hidden in blind spots and move up beside you quickly.
A road area where the speed limit is 30 miles per hour, common in built-up areas in the UK.
Move the car forward very slowly, a little at a time, to improve your view before joining the road.
Places where roads meet or cross; smaller road users can be harder to spot there.
Yellow zig-zag lines near crossings or schools where you must not park or stop and block the view.
A pedestrian crossing with black-and-white stripes where drivers must give way to people waiting to cross.
A trained person (often called a lollipop person) who helps children cross safely near schools.
A sudden change of direction to avoid something, such as a pothole or slippery patch.
When motorcyclists or cyclists move carefully between lanes or past slow queues of traffic.
Briefly switching headlights on and off to attract attention; not a reliable way to give instructions.
Low-powered two-wheel motor vehicles, lighter and slower than most motorcycles.
Orange warning lights that flash to alert drivers, often near schools when children may be about.
A triangular sign showing children, warning that a school is nearby and extra care is needed.
Areas where motor vehicles are normally not allowed and only people on foot may use the space.
A place near a school where children cross the road, often with special signs or a crossing patrol.
In the UK, the lane nearest the left-hand side of the road (kerb side) for normal driving.
A rear-view mirror setting that reduces glare from headlights behind you at night.
More at risk of injury in a collision because of little physical protection (e.g. bikes, motorcycles, pedestrians).
The person who controls railway signals and barriers at a level crossing.
Small, low-power lights used to make a parked or moving vehicle more visible.
An unbroken white road marking that often means you must not cross or enter.
Yellow road markings at the kerb that restrict waiting or parking.
